20                          I.   INTRODUCTION                                  
21        THIS  MATTER  is  before  the  Court  on  Defendant  Express  Scripts,  Inc.  and 
22   Defendant Evernorth Health’s s Motion to Transfer or in the Alternative Dismiss or Strike 
23   the Complaint (“Defendants’ Motion”). Dkt. # 77.  Plaintiffs oppose transfer and dismissal. 
24   Dkt. # 82.  Defendants request oral argument, but the Court finds it unnecessary.  For the 
25   reasons stated below, the Court GRANTS in part and DENIES in part Defendants’ Motion. 
26   Dkt. # 77.                                                                
27                                                                             
1                          II.  BACKGROUND                                    
2        A.   Procedural Background                                           
3        Plaintiffs brought this class action lawsuit in the Western District of Washington 
4   against  Express  Scripts  Inc.  (“ESI”)  and  its  parent  company,  Evernorth  Health  Inc. 
5   (collectively, “Defendants”).  Dkt. # 1.  Plaintiffs filed the First Amended Complaint 
6   (“FAC”) in this matter on March 1, 2024.  Dkt. # 46.  Defendants’ Motion was filed 
7   thereafter, and the parties completed the briefing on this motion on July 22, 2024.  Plaintiffs 
8   filed a Notice of Supplemental Authority on January 24, 2025, Dkt. # 84, and Defendants 
9   filed a response, Dkt. # 85, on February 3, 2025.1                        
10                                                                             
         B.   Factual Background                                              
11                                                                             
          Plaintiffs, a group of pharmacies, challenge agreements that Defendant ESI, a large 
12                                                                             
    pharmacy benefit manager (“PBM”), made with each of the alleged Co-Conspirators. The 
13                                                                             
    Co-Conspirators are three smaller PBMs, Prime, Benecard, and Magellan.  Plaintiffs assert 
14                                                                             
    that agreements constitute a horizontal price-fixing scheme in violation of the Shearman 
15                                                                             
    Act.  The Court summarizes the allegations below.                         
16        The Complaint states that three PBMs, ESI, CVS Caremark, and OptumRx, control 
17   more than 80% of the prescriptions filled in the United States, which means pharmacies 
18   must contract with these three PBMs in order to effectively serve their patients.  Dkt. # 46 
19   ¶¶ 5–7.  Smaller PBMs, such as the Co-Conspirators, have substantially less market share 
20   than  the  three  aforementioned  PBMs,  and  have  ordinarily  and  historically  offered 
21   pharmacies more favorable and competitive reimbursement rates and fees.  Id. ¶¶ 10–12.

1        Plaintiffs identify three of ESI’s contracts with each Co-Conspirator, as horizontal 
2   price-fixing agreements.  Plaintiffs allege that each agreememt fixes the Co-Conspirator’s

1                        III.  LEGAL STANDARDS                                
2        A.   Motion to Dismiss                                               
3        The question for the Court on a motion to dismiss is whether the facts alleged in the 
4   complaint sufficiently state a “plausible” ground for relief.  Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 
5   550 U.S. 544, 570, 167 L.Ed.2d 929 (2007).   In the context of a motion under Rule 
6   12(b)(6), the Court must “accept factual allegations in the complaint as true and construe 
7   the pleadings in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party.”  Manzarek v. St. Paul 
8   Fire & Marine Ins. Co., 519 F.3d 1025, 1031 (9th Cir. 2008) (citation omitted). The Court’s 
9   review is generally limited to the contents of the complaint.  Campanelli v. Bockrath, 100 
10   F.3d 1476, 1479 (9th Cir. 1996).  Courts are not required “to accept as true allegations that 
11   contradict exhibits attached to the Complaint or matters properly subject to judicial notice, 
12   or allegations that are merely conclusory, unwarranted deductions of fact, or unreasonable 
13   inferences.”  Daniels-Hall v. Nat’l Educ. Ass’n, 629 F.3d 992, 998 (9th Cir. 2010). 
14        B.   Motion to Transfer                                              
15        Under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a), “[f]or the convenience of the parties and witnesses, in 
16   the interest of justice, a district court may transfer any civil action to any other district . . .  
17   where it might have been brought.”  The purpose of § 1404 is to prevent wasted time, 
18   energy, and money and to protect litigants, witnesses, and the public from unnecessary 
19   inconvenience and expense.  Van Dusen v. Barrack, 376 U.S. 612, 616 (1964). 
20        A valid forum selection clause may be enforced via a motion to transfer brought 
21   under § 1404(a).  Atl. Marine Const. Co. v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for W. Dist. of Texas, 571 U.S. 
22   49, 59 (2013).  “When the parties have agreed to a valid forum-selection clause, a district 
23   court should ordinarily transfer the case to the forum specified in that clause.”  Id. at 62.  
24   When a valid forum selection clause exists, only “extraordinary circumstances unrelated 
25   to the convenience of the parties” justify denying a § 1404(a) motion.  Id. 
26                                                                             
27                                                                             
                            IV.  DISCUSSION                                   
1        A.   Transfer                                                        
2        Defendants argue that Plaintiffs’ claims are subject to a forum-selection clause 
3   pursuant to their Pharmacy Provider Agreements with ESI.  Dkt. # 77 at 13.  Plaintiffs do 
4   not dispute the validity of the of the forum-selection clause, rather they argue that the 
5   claims in this matter fall outside the scope of the provision in the agreements.  See Dkt. # 
6   82 at 4–8.   In opposing transfer, Plaintiffs cite to CZ Servs., Inc. v. Express Scripts Holding 
7   Co., No. 18-cv-04217, 2018 WL 3972030, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 20, 2018) (“CZ Services”).  
8   See id.  Although Defendants acknowledge that the case “involve[es] the same forum-
9   selection clause,” Defendants contend the circumstances are distinguishable.  See Dkt. # 
10   83 at 3.                                                                  
11        The relevant agreements between each Plaintiff and Express Scripts contains a 
12   nearly identical “Dispute Resolution” provision that includes a forum-selection clause.  
13   Plaintiff Osterhaus Pharmacy’s Provider Agreement provides that:          
14                                                                             
         Except as provided herein, prior to either party taking any legal action in connection with 
15        this Agreement, both parties agree to meet in good faith to resolve any claim or controversy 
         (“Claim”). Whether under federal or state statutory or common law, brought by either ESI 
16        or the Provider against the other, or against the employee, members, agents or assigns of 
         the other, arising from or relating in any way to the interpretation or performance of this 
17        Agreement . . .  All litigation between the parties arising out of or related in any way to 
         the interpretation or performance of the Agreement shall be litigated in the U.S. District 
18        Court for the Eastern District of Missouri, or as to those lawsuits which the Court lacks 
         jurisdiction, before a court located in St. Louis County Missouri.  The parties agree that 
19        Claims shall not be consolidated or coordinated in any action with the Claim of any other 
         individual or entity. No Claim or other dispute may be litigated on a coordinated, class, 
20        mass, or consolidated basis.                                         
21   Dkt. # 78-2 at 4 (emphasis added).                                        
22        A forum-selection clause is properly enforced through 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a), which 
23   codifies the doctrine of forum non conveniens “for the subset of cases in which the 
24   transferee forum is within the federal court system.”  Atl. Marine, 571 U.S. at 60; see also 
25   28 U.S.C. § 1404(a). Section 1404(a) provides that, “[f]or the convenience of the parties 
26   and witnesses, in the interest of justice, a district court may transfer any civil action to any 
27                                                                             
1   other district . . . where it may have been brought or to any district  . . . to which all parties 
2   have consented.”  28 U.S.C. § 1404(a). Typically, a forum-selection clause is enforced 
3   upon a motion to transfer.  See, e.g., Atl. Marine, 571 U.S. at 59.       
4        Forum-selection clauses “can be equally applicable to contractual and tort causes of 
5   action.”  Manetti–Farrow, Inc. v. Gucci Am., Inc., 858 F.2d 509, 514 (9th Cir. 1988). 
6   Forum-selection clauses do not apply to any and all litigation between the parties. See In 
7   re Orange, S.A., 818 F.3d 956, 962 (9th Cir. 2016).  They apply only to the claims in that 
8   will require the interpretation of the agreements, or a determination of whether the parties 
9   complied with their terms.  Id. at 963.                                   
10        Where,  for  example,  the  clause  governs  claims  “arising  under”  the  particular 
11   agreement that contains the forum selection clause, it “should be interpreted narrowly,” 
12   i.e., as applying only to those disputes “relating to the interpretation and performance of 
13   the contract itself.”  Cape Flattery Ltd. v. Titan Maritime, LLC, 647 F.3d 914, 922 (9th Cir. 
14   2011) (quoting Mediterranean Enters., Inc. v. Ssangyong Corp., 708 F.2d 1458, 1464 (9th 
15   Cir. 1983).  By contrast, a clause that provides that all disputes “arising out of or relating 
16   to” or “in connection with” an agreement shall be adjudicated in a specified forum is 
17   broader.  See id.                                                         
18        In CZ Services, a Northern District of California court found that a forum-selection 
19   clause, the same clause at issue here, did not apply to Plaintiffs’ defamation claims.  The 
20   court stated: “The determinative question is whether the [] claims will require the Court or 
21   the trier of fact to make any findings about the adequacy of the parties’ performance under 
22   the provider agreements.”  Defendants contend that the court in CZ Services found that the 
23   defamation claims fell outside of the forum-selection clause because the claims would 
24   “stand or fall without any reference to the agreement.”  Dkt. # 83 at 8.  Further, Defendants 
25   assert this Court should enforce the clause because “Plaintiffs’ Complaint is built on 
26   express references to the rates, fees, and pricing schedules set out in the Agreements.”  Id.  
27                                                                             
1        Defendants attempt to distinguish CZ Services is unavailing.  Although the language 
2   of the clause signals that it should be interpreted broadly, the clause itself is inapplicable 
3   because  Plaintiffs  are  not  disputing  ESI’s  reimbursement  rates  and  fees  with  the 
4   pharmacies.  At most, the claims concern Plaintiffs’ agreements with Co-Conspirators, 
5   non-parties in this action.  These agreements are separate and unrelated to ESI’s Pharmacy 
6   Provider Agreements with Plaintiffs.  Thus, Plaintiffs’ antitrust claims can be adjudicated 
7   without any reference to ESI’s agreements, and the case can stay with this Court. 
8        Defendants’ argument regarding the class action claims fails for the same reasons 
9   that the Court discussed above.  The class claims do not relate to the interpretation or 
10   performance of the Pharmacy Provider Agreements.  The claims relate to ESI’s conduct 
11   with Co-Conspirator PBMs, which Plaintiffs allege resulted in pharmacies paying inflated 
12   fees and recouping depressed reimbursements from the Co-Conspirator PBMs, not ESI.  
13   Therefore, the Court will not strike the class allegations.               
14        B.   Dismissal of Antitrust Claims                                   
15        Defendants argue that the Court should dismiss the Complaint because Plaintiffs 
16   fail to state an antitrust injury necessary for standing and fail to state a claim for which 
17   relief can be granted under Section 1 of the Sherman Act.  See generally Dkts. # 77, 83.  
18        Under Section 1 of the Sherman Act, “[e]very contract, combination in the form of 
19   trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States 
20   . . .  is declared to be illegal.”  15 U.S.C. § 1.  The Supreme Court has held that while 
21   Section 1 prohibits every agreement “in restraint of trade,” the Court “has long recognized 
22   that Congress intended to outlaw only unreasonable restraints.”  State Oil Co. v. Khan, 522 
23   U.S. 3, 10 (1997).  Under Section 1, a plaintiff must prove that (1) an agreement exists, (2) 
24   the agreement imposed an unreasonable restraint of trade through either a per se or rule of 
25   reason analysis, and (3) the restraint affected interstate commerce.  Am. Ad Mgmt., Inc. v. 
26   GTE Corp., 92 F.3d 781, 784 (9th Cir. 1996).                              
27                                                                             
1             1.   Antitrust Injury                                           
2        The Court first turns to whether Plaintiffs have plausibly asserted a cognizable 
3   antirust  injury.  Defendants  argue  that  Plaintiffs  failed  to  allege  PBMs  are  economic 
4   “substitutes,” and thus failed to establish an antitrust injury.  See Dkt. # 83 at 11–12. 
5   Defendants also argue that Plaintiffs fail to establish an antitrust injury because the network 
6   rental agreements increased competition and allowed Co-Conspirator PBMs to offer lower 
7   drug prices.  Dkt. # 77 at 11.  As a result of the agreements, Defendants assert that 
8   consumers, health plans and those insured by health plans, benefit from reduced prices.  
9   See id.                                                                   
10        To establish an antitrust injury, a plaintiff must show an injury “causally linked” to 
11   an alleged anti-competitive practice, and that the injury is one that “the antitrust laws were 
12   intended to prevent and that flows from that which makes the defendants’ acts unlawful.” 
13   Cargill, Inc. v. Monfort of Colo., Inc., 479 U.S. 104, 109 (1986) (quoting Brunswick Corp. 
14   v. Pueblo Bowl-O-Mat, Inc., 429 U.S. 477, 489 (1977)).   Antitrust liability can arise from 
15   a horizontal conspiracy whereby a defendant agrees with others to fix prices “caus[ing] 
16   buyers to pay more, or sellers to receive less, than the prices that would prevail in a market 
17   free of the unlawful trade restraint.”  Knevelbaard Dairies v. Kraft Foods, Inc., 232 F.3d 
18   979, 988 (9th Cir. 2000); see also W. Penn Allegheny Health Sys., Inc. v. UPMC, 627 F.3d 
19   85, 103 (3d Cir. 2010).                                                   
20        The caselaw Defendants use to support that Plaintiff must demonstrate that PBMs 
21   are substitutes is not analogous to the circumstances alleged in this matter.  For example, 
22   in Intel Corp. v. Fortress Inv. Grp. LLC, the court dismissed claims in part for failure to 
23   adequately plead an antitrust injury.  No. 19-cv-07651, 2020 WL 6390499, (N.D. Cal. July 
24   15, 2020) (“Intel Corp.”).  There, Apple and Intel Corporation, asserted antitrust claims 
25   against  companies  alleged  to  have  aggregated  a  portfolio  of  “weak”  patents  that 
26   aggressively  enforced  those  patents  through  infringement  actions.    See  id.  at  *1.  
27                                                                             
1   Essentially, the Complaint alleged that the aggregation of a broad array of patents stifles 
2   competition of electronic device suppliers and eliminates substitutes.  See id. at *2.  When 
3   analyzing the relevant market, the court noted that Plaintiffs failed to explain how patents 
4   for a smartphone a part of the same market as a refrigerator could be when the products are 
5   not substitutes themselves.  See id. at *9.  When analyzing whether an antitrust injury was 
6   present, the court concluded there was “was no clear injury it is not clear that those lawsuits 
7   came about because of the elimination of substitutes.”  Id. at *12 (emphasis in original). 
8        The circumstances of Intel Corp. are patently distinguishable from this case.  First, 
9   that case does not concern a horizontal price-fixing conspiracy.  Second, the case involved 
10   a somewhat novel strategy to use antitrust law to challenge meritless patent litigation.  
11   Third,  Plaintiffs  in  this  case  did  not  put  substitutes  at  issue  in  their  allegations.  
12   Accordingly, to the extent the Court need address “substitutes” or decide whether PBMs 
13   are “competitors” at this stage of litigation, the Court concludes that the description of the 
14   companies alleged in the Complaint and common sense indicate the PBMs are competitors 
15   and substitutes as they provide identical services to pharmacies.         
16        Defendants also argue that the agreements benefit consumers, so pharmacies cannot 
17   base an antitrust injury on this basis.  Dkt. # 77 at 18.  However, these facts contradict the 
18   facts of the Complaint, which is improper on a motion to dismiss.  Therefore, the Court 
19   will not dismiss on that basis.                                           
20        The Court is satisfied that these agreements between ESI and Co-Conspirators, to 
21   share the large firm’s market power, allowed Co-Conspirators to receive more favorable 
22   rates and reimbursements at the expense of Plaintiffs, and plausibly at the expense of 
23   consumers.  Plaintiffs’ injuries are “causally linked” because the injury stems from Co-
24   Conspirators change of rates to match ESI’s rates, that would not have prevailed in the free 
25   market absent the restraint of trade.  Accordingly, the Court concludes Plaintiffs have 
26   established an antitrust injury.                                          
27                                                                             
              1.   § 1 Shearman Act                                           
1                                                                             
         The Court now turns to whether Plaintiffs’ assertions are sufficient to establish a 
2                                                                             
    plausible claim for relief under § 1 of the Shearman Act.  Plaintiffs contend that the network 
3                                                                             
    rental agreements between ESI and each PBM Co-Conspirator constitute a per se violation 
4                                                                             
    of Section 1.  Dkt. # 46 ¶¶ 40–70.  Plaintiffs allege that these agreements are horizontal 
5                                                                             
    price-fixing agreements because after they were made, the Co-Conspirators uniformly 
6                                                                             
    changed  their  fees  and  reimbursement  rates  to  match  the  higher  rates  that  ESI  has 
7                                                                             
    historically charged.  Defendants do not dispute that horizontal price-fixing is considered 
8                                                                             
    per  se  unlawful.    Rather,  Defendants  argue  that  PBMs  are  “effectively  purchasing 
9                                                                             
    cooperatives,” immune from per se antitrust scrutiny.  See Dkt. # 77 at 19.  In support of 
10                                                                             
    this argument Defendants do not refer to the facts as they are alleged in the Complaint, but, 
11                                                                             
    instead, they point to caselaw describing the function of PBMs.  See id. at 19–21. 
12                                                                             
         In analyzing the reasonableness of an agreement under Section 1, the Supreme Court 
13                                                                             
    has distinguished between agreements made between competitors (horizontal agreements) 
14                                                                             
    and agreements made up and down a supply chain, such as between a retailer and a 
15                                                                             
    manufacturer (vertical agreements). See In re Musical Instruments & Equip. Antitrust 
16                                                                             
    Litig.,  798  F.3d  1186,  1191  (9th  Cir.  2015)  (“Musical  Instruments”).    Horizontal 
17                                                                             
    agreements in which competitors fix prices, divide markets, or refuse to deal are per se 
18                                                                             
    violations of the Sherman Act.   Id.  “Once the agreement’s existence is established, no 
19                                                                             
    further inquiry into the practice’s actual effect on the market or the parties’ intentions is 
20                                                                             
    necessary to establish a § 1 violation.”  Id.                             
21                                                                             
         Plaintiffs must provide “plausible grounds to infer an agreement,” Twombly, 550 
22                                                                             
    U.S. at 556, 127, but they are not required to show that an agreement is probable or to 
23                                                                             
    “allege a fact pattern that tends to exclude the possibility of lawful, independent conduct,” 
24                                                                             
    SmileDirectClub, LLC v. Tippins, 31 F.4th 1110 (9th Cir. 2022) (quoting Erie Cnty. v. 
25                                                                             
    Morton Salt, Inc., 702 F.3d 860, 869 (6th Cir. 2012)).  Evidence of concerted, rather than 
26                                                                             
    independent, action among market competitors can include direct evidence of horizontal 
27                                                                             
1   agreements between competitors, Musical Instruments, 798 F.3d at 1193, the acceptance 
2   of an invitation to participate in a common scheme that restrains trade, Interstate Cir. v. 
3   United States, 306 U.S. 208, 227(1939); PLS.Com, LLC v. Nat’l Ass’n of Realtors, 32 F.4th 
4   824, 843 (9th Cir. 2022), or the existence of parallel conduct coupled with some further 
5   factual circumstance pointing towards a meeting of the minds, Musical Instruments, 798 
6   F.3d at 1194.                                                             
7        A per se analysis applies when “the practice facially appears to be one that would 
8   always or almost always tend to restrict competition and decrease output.”  Am. Ad. Mgmt. 
9   Inc., 92 F.3d at 784.  “Per se liability is reserved for only those agreements that are so 
10   plainly anticompetitive that no elaborate study of the industry is needed to establish their 
11   illegality.”  Texaco Inc. v. Dagher, 547 U.S. 1, 5 (2006). The Supreme Court has held that 
12   “a combination formed for the purpose and with the effect of raising, depressing, fixing, 
13   pegging, or stabilizing the price of a commodity in interstate or foreign commerce is illegal 
14   per se.”  Palmer v. BRG of Georgia, Inc., 498 U.S. 46, 48 (1990) (citing United States v. 
15   Socony-Vacuum Oil Co., 310 U.S. 150, 223).  To justify a per se prohibition, a restraint 
16   must have “manifestly anticompetitive” effects.  Cont’l T. V., Inc. v. GTE Sylvania Inc., 
17   433 U.S. 36, 50 (1977).  Horizontal price-fixing is “ordinarily condemned as unreasonable 
18   per se” and is “‘perhaps the paradigm of an unreasonable restraint of trade.’”  In re ATM 
19   Fee Antitrust Litig., 554 F. Supp. 2d 1003, 1014 (N.D. Cal. 2008) (quoting Nat’l Collegiate 
20   Athletic Ass’n v. Bd. of Regents of Univ. of Oklahoma, 468 U.S. 85, 100 (1984)). 
21        The existence of these network rental agreements is alleged in the Complaint and 
22   does not appear to be disputed by Defendants.  See generally Dkts. # 46, 77, 83.   The Court 
23   accepts Plaintiffs allegations as true and finds that Plaintiffs have sufficiently demonstrated 
24   that ESI and the Co-Conspirators had a contract which is clearly sufficient for the Court to 
25   plausibly infer an agreement.                                             
26                                                                             
27                                                                             
1        Despite the existence of the agreements, Defendants argue ESI and Co-Conspirators 
2   are joint purchasers rather than competitors and thus are not subject to per se antitrust 
3   scrutiny.  Much of the caselaw cited by Defendants in support of this argument had a 
4   different procedural posture than this matter.  See, e.g., Stop & Shop Supermarket Co. v. 
5   Blue Cross & Blue Shield of R.I., 373 F.3d 57 (1st Cir. 2004) (reviewing a district court’s 
6   grant of summary judgment for plaintiffs’ per se claims under Section 1 of the Shearman 
7   Act against PBMs and insurers); In re EpiPen (Epinephrine Injection, USP) Mktg., Sales 
8   Pracs. & Antitrust Litig., 44 F.4th 959, 966 (10th Cir. 2022) (discussing role of PBMs in 
9   affirming a district court’s grant of summary judgment in favor of defendants for claims 
10   brought  by  pharmaceutical  companies  under  Section  2  of  the  Shearman  Act);  In  re 
11   Pharmacy Benefit Managers Antitrust Litig., 2017 WL 275398, at *4 (E.D. Pa. Jan. 18, 
12   2017) (characterizing PBM administration as achieving “a number of efficiencies” in 
13   years-long litigation in ruling on Daubert motions for pending class certification).  In those 
14   cases, the cases had developed facts where it was appropriate for a court to look beyond 
15   the Complaint.  Further, it does not follow from the fact that PBMs act as joint purchasers 
16   in one context that PBMs act as joint purchasers in every context.  The Court declines to 
17   adopt factual determinations made in other PBM antitrust disputes that had different 
18   allegations and parties to support the conclusion that PBMs are purchasing cooperatives 
19   rather than competitors in this context.3                                 
20        Further, “[t]he [cooperative buying defense] should generally be rejected where 
21   there is no integration of agency services, negotiation, contracting, or delivery, but that the 
22   firms have simply agreed on a price.”  Phillip E. Areeda & Herbert Hovenkamp, Antitrust 
23   Law: An Analysis of Antitrust Principles and Their Application § 2012b (2022 ed.).  The 
24   Complaint indicates that the network rental agreements have not generated any efficiencies 
25   or integration and the only joint activity is price-fixing.  See Dkt. # 46 ¶¶ 52–54, 57, 60.  
26                                                                             

27   3 For the reasons discussed in Section IV.B.1 supra, it is plausible that PBMs are competitors. 
1   The  Complaint  references  a  Prime  executive’s  interview  that  indicates  ESI  and  Co-
2   Conspirator, Prime act independently.  See id. ¶ 52–54.  Defendants ask the Court to look 
3   at the interview in its entirety to demonstrate that achieved cost saving measures for clients.  
4   See Dkt. # 83 at 13; see also Dkt. # 78-1.  However, looking at the interview, it neither 
5   conclusively proves that any savings were passed off to consumers, nor does it demonstrate 
6   that there was any integration that would refute per se antitrust scrutiny.  Considering 
7   Defendants’ dispute of the facts in the Complaint and the procedural posture of this case, 
8   it would be inappropriate for the Court to consider Defendants’ characterization of ESI as 
9   a “joint purchaser” rather than a direct competitor at this stage of the litigation.4   
10        The Complaint plausibly alleges that the network rental agreements are a horizontal 
11   price-fixing scheme. The Complaint demonstrates that ESI and Co-Conspirators matched 
12   their rates and fees after they entered into the network rental agreements and ESI and Co-
13   Conspirators provide the same services to pharmacies.  These allegations, taken as true 
14   plausibly indicate a price-fixing scheme that is an unreasonable restraint of trade that 
15   antitrust laws forbid.                                                    
16        Accordingly, Plaintiffs have met the burdens of asserting a per se antitrust violation 
17   for horizontal price-fixing.  Therefore, the Court will not dismiss Plaintiffs’ antitrust claims 
18   under §1 of the Shearman Act at this time.  The Court notes that it need not separately 
19   analyze Plaintiffs claims under the rule of reason at this time as it concludes Plaintiffs 
20   properly pleaded a Section 1 claim. 5  However, if Plaintiffs cannot prove a per se violation
